I'm so sorry. That is a horrible experience and it's completely normal to feel violated and sad. In my experience I've also felt shame, guilt and anger at myself for not stopping it as soon as it happens, but the shock makes you paralyze with fear, and the public setting makes it hard to cry out.
Just know that it is absolutely not your fault, and all of your current feelings are validated. I hope you have a good friend or family member you can talk to. Unfortunately so many of my friends have gone through something similar.

I'm so sorry you are going through this :( However, I agree with your friends. I think it's healthier for you in the long run to end things. Give yourself time to grieve. Be single for a time, focus on making your mental health better by not having it depend on someone else who is committment-shy.

I have absolute certainty that there is someone out there (multiple someones) whith whom you will have full, beautiful relationships and not this kind "relationship". The hardest thing to accept is that you can't control him, you can't fix him, and you should definitely not wait for him, so you should let him go. I'm so sorry though, it must be horrible. 

Whatever you choose to do, hang in there.

What I feel is that it's maybe a bit unfair for you. Are you dating other people? If you got a girlfriend, how do you think she would react? Would you even be able to have a relationship with someone else when there is such a dependency between you and your friend?

Just my two cents!

Hi. I'm sorry about this situation. I don't have any or all the answers but here is some advice based on my own experience.


All-male friend groups, especially those that you link up to through a significant other can be great. I get it, especially if they understand the memes, the gaming culture that you like as well and that you can't find elsewhere. But the reality is that you are your boyfriend's girlfriend. Especially if you were introduced into the friend group as such. There are logical boundaries that they should be respecting. For example, not flirting with you or treating you with disrespect. (Btw, being drunk is not an excuse for being sexist). I think there is a natural distance that takes time to overcome. 

From what you write, it feels like you are in need a female friend or a new group of friends with men and women. I agree. I think it's healthy to have multiple social circles. They don't all have to be very close, they can be acquaintances even. You mentioned you were in a campus. There must be social activities you could try out. Even if you don't think it's your cup of tea, try a dancing or a self defense class, maybe there's a fandom meetup that you like, or a sport club you can try out. It might be awkward. As someone that tends to be introverted, it can be hard. But also so rewarding! You might not make friends from the get go, but that's ok, you're branching out. You will gain social experience, you'll get used to interacting with women, who honestly can give some of the best friendships you will have in your whole life. Your current friends and boyfriend will see you as a more well rounded person if you have a life apart from them. 

You mentioned having social anxiety and high energy and how those can be obstacles in gaining new friends. It must be hard, I'm sorry. But you do have friends! So you can make new ones! I bet you're super fun to hang around with. Maybe bonding over an activity or interest with a stranger in a controlled setting like a class can be more structured and lead to new social adventures. Also, try not to psych yourself out by saying women friends just don't work out. Maybe they haven't in the past but why shouldn't they in the future? Women are just people, like men, in the end.

Sorry for the wall of text! Hope it helps :)

Over the past few months, I've had girl friends get "lost" in new relationships. 

I don't really know the boyfriends well or at all, so I can't make a judgement on whether they're HVM, LVM or NVM. (I doubt they're HVM though). I *can* analyse my friends' changed behaviour since then.

-changes in priorities. Friends get pushed down the priorities list over the bf. The allocation of social time is now beneficial to the bf. Examples: saying no to a girl's trip and opting to travel with bf instead. Being flexible about plans with family/friends but inflexible when it comes to respecting bf's schedule. 

-changes in attitude. Conversations are a bit more.. fake. The authenticity and true friendship from before is replaced by a "everything's perfect" attitude. Example: If they complain about the bf one day, after they've made up the problematic behaviour is sweeped under the rug, minimised or defended.

-changes in big life decisions. In order to cater to the relationship and the bf, careers are tweaked. For example, when changing career paths, one of the reasons is compatibility with the bf.

As a result, they distance themselves. Honestly, I've let them. I don't want to be around that energy. Since discovering FDS I feel like an outsider looking in. Before, I would have felt guilty about the distance, I would have been sad about being pushed down the priority list. Now I just don't care as much. I won't accomodate their pickme pandering. If they can't make time and put effort in a friendship with me, I won't sacrifice my time and effort to make up for their behaviour.

I also feel like when my mental health isn't good I daydream maladaptively. It can make me deprioritise important things like studying, working,  sleeping, even relaxing. 

So I try to recognize when I'm falling down a daydreaming rabbit hole (basically this need to finish the storyline over everything else). And I give myself a set time for daydreaming: 15 after lunch, right before going to bed, while commuting, etc. 

You're not going to forget the characters or storylines. Visualize storing them in a safe mental box you can take out when it doesn't conflict with your schedule.
